headline: Hotels sue Booking, Marriott staff reapply, Your lobby gets lawyers and more! (I have notes)
tldr: 18,135 hotels have signed up to drag Booking to court over twenty years of parity clauses, and the commission invoice (naturally) still lands on time. Marriott posted RevPAR up 6.5% and thanked some corporate staff by inviting them to reapply for their own desks, while an intruder spent three years browsing reservation data at Amadeus without once checking out. A U.K. bill hands mayors uncapped holiday taxes, Airbnb put $7.1 million into Los Angeles elections, and Michael O'Leary told analysts a pilot strike would save Ryanair money. Add ADA plaintiffs sniffing around your lobby fragrance, and you have a week in which the best-performing asset class was the lawsuit.
notice: Welcome back, audience. The Sunday 08:00 safety net has now finalized the shortlist 2 weeks running, so if you enjoy this issue the credit goes to Michael and if you hate it the complaint goes to me.

stories.title: 18,135 hotels would like their parity money back
stories.text: 18,135 hotels have now signed up to drag Booking Holdings before the Amsterdam District Court, up from 3,087 in January and 68% more than three months ago (turns out resentment compounds nicely).

stories.title: Your per-key spreadsheet can't price a feeling
stories.text: Boutique owners Ferial Sadeghian and Jayson Seidman looked at the sacred per-key metric and suggested breaking it apart. Heresy, and about time. They also say to protect your atmosphere budget and to expect F&B to outweigh rooms revenue.

stories.title: Your OTA guests are one-night stands
stories.text: Direct guests return at 5.1%, OTA guests at 1.3%. Same hotels, same rooms, same front desk, across 2.2 million guests at European hotel groups in Bookboost's data. So no, your night auditor's charm is not the variable.

stories.title: Three-year stay, no check-in. Congratulations, Amadeus.
stories.text: August 2023 to September 2026. That's how long an unauthorized party browsed reservation data in Amadeus systems, and Cathay Pacific says they used credentials assigned to an Amadeus system account (a valid key card, basically).
